claim: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular, gram-negative human pathogen that infects hundreds of millions of people every year to cause trachoma and blindness or sexually transmitted diseases (STD), which can lead to ectopic pregnancy and infertility.
source: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular, gram-negative human pathogen that infects hundreds of millions of people every year to cause trachoma and blindness or sexually transmitted diseases (STD), which can lead to ectopic pregnancy and infertility.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about C. trachomatis epidemiology and disease outcomes.

claim: Chlamydia has a biphasic life-cycle starting with the infection of the host cell by the non-replicating elementary body (EB).
source: Chlamydia has a biphasic life-cycle starting with the infection of the host cell by the non-replicating elementary body (EB).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Chlamydia developmental cycle.

claim: Once the EB entered the cell, it differentiates into the metabolic active reticulate body (RB) and replicates inside a vacuole, the so-called chlamydial inclusion.
source: Once the EB entered the cell, it differentiates into the metabolic active reticulate body (RB) and replicates inside a vacuole, the so-called chlamydial inclusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Chlamydia developmental cycle.

claim: The RBs re-differentiate into the infectious EBs, which are released by host cell lysis or extrusion.
source: To complete the developmental cycle, the RBs re-differentiate into the infectious EBs, which are released by host cell lysis or extrusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Chlamydia developmental cycle.

claim: During replication, the bacteria secrete several effector proteins through type two- (T2SS) or three-secretion systems (T3SS) to intrude in cellular processes for their benefit.
source: During replication, the bacteria secrete several effector proteins through type two- (T2SS) or three-secretion systems (T3SS) to intrude in cellular processes for their benefit (Subtil et al., 2005; Valdivia, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Inc proteins in general interact with numerous different host proteins thereby orchestrating processes like vesicular trafficking and signaling cascades essential for inclusion formation and bacterial replication.
source: Inc proteins in general interact with numerous different host proteins thereby orchestrating processes like vesicular trafficking and signaling cascades essential for inclusion formation and bacterial replication (Elwell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Chlamydia established strategies to prevent apoptosis to sustain their favored environment.
source: Due to the full dependence on the host cell for replication, Chlamydia established strategies to prevent apoptosis to sustain their favored environment (Sharma and Rudel, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: During bacterial entry into the host cell, the Raf/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT survival signaling pathways are activated that in turn mediate the transcriptional up-regulation and stabilization of the anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family member Mcl-1.
source: During bacterial entry into the host cell, the Raf/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT survival signaling pathways are activated that in turn mediate the transcriptional up-regulation and stabilization of the anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family member Mcl-1 (Rajalingam et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In C. trachomatis-mediated apoptosis resistance in human cells, Mcl-1 is crucial because depletion of Mcl-1 sensitizes infected cells to cell death.
source: In C. trachomatis-mediated apoptosis resistance in human cells, Mcl-1 is crucial because depletion of Mcl-1 sensitizes infected cells to cell death (Rajalingam et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2011; Rödel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ubiquitin ligases MULE and the SCFFbw7 complex as well as the deubiquitinating enzyme USP9X mainly control the protein turnover of Mcl-1.
source: Here, the ubiquitin ligases MULE and the SCFFbw7 complex as well as the deubiquitinating enzyme USP9X mainly control the protein turnover of Mcl-1 (Zhong et al., 2005; Ding et al., 2007; Inuzuka et al., 2011; Schwickart et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is so far unknown by which mechanism C. trachomatis stabilize Mcl-1 upon infection.
source: However, it is so far unknown by which mechanism C. trachomatis stabilize Mcl-1 upon infection.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The chlamydial effector proteins ChlaDUB1 (CTL0247) and ChlaDUB2 (CTL0246), in the following termed Cdu1 and Cdu2, were demonstrated to have in vitro deubiquitinating and deneddylating activity.
source: The chlamydial effector proteins ChlaDUB1 (CTL0247) and ChlaDUB2 (CTL0246), in the following termed Cdu1 and Cdu2, were demonstrated to have in vitro deubiquitinating and deneddylating activity (Misaghi et al., 2006; Pruneda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One of the Cdu1 targets was suggested to be IκBα, which may prevent NFκB signaling and immune response to ensure survival inside the host cell.
source: One of the Cdu1 targets was suggested to be IκBα, which may prevent NFκB signaling and immune response to ensure survival inside the host cell (Le Negrate et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cdu1 enzyme was shown to localize to the inclusion membrane and stabilize Mcl-1 by deubiquitination.
source: In this study, Cdu1 enzyme was shown to localize to the inclusion membrane and stabilize Mcl-1 by deubiquitination.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mcl-1 protein levels decline only marginally in cells infected with a Cdu1 mutant strain of Chlamydia.
source: However, Mcl-1 protein levels decline only marginally in cells infected with a Cdu1 mutant strain of Chlamydia suggesting that keeping high Mcl-1 levels is regulated at multiple levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Keeping high Mcl-1 levels is regulated at multiple levels.
source: However, Mcl-1 protein levels decline only marginally in cells infected with a Cdu1 mutant strain of Chlamydia suggesting that keeping high Mcl-1 levels is regulated at multiple levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Mcl-1 levels decline only marginally in Cdu1 mutant-infected cells.

claim: The Cdu1 mutant was severely affected in its development upon IFNγ challenge in vitro.
source: Interestingly, the Cdu1 mutant was severely affected in its development upon IFNγ challenge in vitro and survival in mouse genital infections.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The Cdu1 mutant was severely affected in survival in mouse genital infections.
source: Interestingly, the Cdu1 mutant was severely affected in its development upon IFNγ challenge in vitro and survival in mouse genital infections.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Mcl-1 protein levels strongly increase upon 16 hr post infection (hpi) and remain high until the end of the chlamydial developmental cycle.
source: Mcl-1 protein levels strongly increase upon 16 hr post infection (hpi) and remain high until the end of the chlamydial developmental cycle.
evidence: This is a known observation from prior research.

claim: Augmented Mcl-1 levels are the result of increased protein expression initially triggered by the Raf/MEK/ERK and the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway.
source: Augmented Mcl-1 levels are the result of increased protein expression initially triggered by the Raf/MEK/ERK and the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway (Rajalingam et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Preventing Mcl-1 de novo protein synthesis by treatment of the cells with cycloheximide (CHX) or decreasing MCL1 gene transcription by blocking MEK/ERK signaling with the inhibitor UO126 revealed extended stabilization of Mcl-1 in infected cells.
source: However, preventing Mcl-1 de novo protein synthesis by treatment of the cells with cycloheximide (CHX) or decreasing MCL1 gene transcription by blocking MEK/ERK signaling with the inhibitor UO126 revealed extended stabilization of Mcl-1 in infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The mechanism of prolonged Mcl-1 stabilization during the replicative stages of C. trachomatis infection is unknown.
source: The mechanism of prolonged Mcl-1 stabilization during the replicative stages of C. trachomatis infection is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Compared to non-stimulated control cells, a mild increase in ubiquitination as a result of apoptosis signaling was detected after TNFα/CHX treatment in uninfected, but not in infected cells.
source: Compared to non-stimulated control cells, a mild increase in ubiquitination as a result of apoptosis signaling was detected after TNFα/CHX treatment in uninfected, but not in infected cells (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: Mcl-1 ubiquitination was reduced in infected cells independently of the TNFα/CHX treatment.
source: Interestingly, Mcl-1 ubiquitination was reduced in infected cells independently of the TNFα/CHX treatment (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Reduced ubiquitination protects Mcl-1 from proteasomal degradation and may lead to Mcl-1 accumulation.
source: Reduced ubiquitination protects Mcl-1 from proteasomal degradation and may lead to Mcl-1 accumulation, as previously observed (Rajalingam et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of reduced ubiquitination and supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Even the mild increase in Mcl-1 levels causes protection from apoptosis induction.
source: Since even the mild increase in Mcl-1 levels causes protection from apoptosis induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), this stabilized Mcl-1 will interfere with apoptosis induction in infected cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Stabilized Mcl-1 will interfere with apoptosis induction in infected cells.
source: Since even the mild increase in Mcl-1 levels causes protection from apoptosis induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), this stabilized Mcl-1 will interfere with apoptosis induction in infected cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mild increases in Mcl-1 protect from apoptosis.

claim: The anti-apoptotic function of Mcl-1 depends on its interaction with pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins to block apoptosis induction.
source: The anti-apoptotic function of Mcl-1 depends on its interaction with pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins to block apoptosis induction (Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Bim is known to interact with Mcl-1.
source: Bim is known to interact with Mcl-1 and both could be co-immunoprecipitated from cells infected with C. trachomatis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) suggesting that Mcl-1 is active in sequestering Bim in infected cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Mcl-1 and Bim interaction.

claim: Bim and Mcl-1 could be co-immunoprecipitated from cells infected with C. trachomatis.
source: Bim is known to interact with Mcl-1 and both could be co-immunoprecipitated from cells infected with C. trachomatis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) suggesting that Mcl-1 is active in sequestering Bim in infected cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mcl-1 is active in sequestering Bim in infected cells.
source: Bim is known to interact with Mcl-1 and both could be co-immunoprecipitated from cells infected with C. trachomatis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) suggesting that Mcl-1 is active in sequestering Bim in infected cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Many cancer cells have increased levels of Mcl-1 protein due to the misregulation of cellular UPS factors like MULE, USP9X and components of the SCFFbw7 complex which promotes apoptosis resistance.
source: Many cancer cells have increased levels of Mcl-1 protein due to the misregulation of cellular UPS factors like MULE, USP9X and components of the SCFFbw7 complex (Schwickart et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2005; Inuzuka et al., 2011) which promotes apoptosis resistance (Zhang et al., 2002; Adams and Cooper, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: All these ubiquitin-modifying proteins were present at similar levels in control and C. trachomatis-infected HeLa cells.
source: However, all these ubiquitin-modifying proteins were present at similar levels in control and C. trachomatis-infected HeLa cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E.

claim: No difference in the protein level of Cullin 1 or its modification by Nedd8 was observed in C. trachomatis-infected cells compared to uninfected control cells.
source: The ubiquitin ligase activity of SCF E3 ligase complexes can be altered by neddylation of the Cullin subunit, but no difference in the protein level of Cullin 1 or its modification by Nedd8 was observed in C. trachomatis-infected cells compared to uninfected control cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Cdu1 is known to be expressed 16 hpi.
source: Cdu1 is known to be expressed 16 hpi (Le Negrate et al., 2008) when Mcl-1 levels start increasing in infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Time course experiments confirmed a simultaneous Mcl-1 stabilization and Cdu1 expression.
source: Time course experiments confirmed a simultaneous Mcl-1 stabilization and Cdu1 expression (Figure 1D), indicating that Cdu1 might be responsible for Mcl-1 stabilization by deubiquitination and protection from proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cdu1 might be responsible for Mcl-1 stabilization by deubiquitination and protection from proteasomal degradation.
source: Time course experiments confirmed a simultaneous Mcl-1 stabilization and Cdu1 expression (Figure 1D), indicating that Cdu1 might be responsible for Mcl-1 stabilization by deubiquitination and protection from proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the temporal correlation between Cdu1 expression and Mcl-1 stabilization.

claim: Sequence alignments clearly allocate Cdu1 into the family C48 of the CE clan of cysteine proteases.
source: Sequence alignments clearly allocate Cdu1 into the family C48 of the CE clan of cysteine proteases.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: The peptidases share a common architecture toward the catalytically active C-terminus, while the N-terminus is weakly conserved.
source: The peptidases share a common architecture toward the catalytically active C-terminus, while the N-terminus is weakly conserved (Mossessova and Lima, 2000) and members include the Ulp1 protease, from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Li and Hochstrasser, 1999) as well as the Sentrin-specific proteases (SENPs) from higher eukaryotes (Yeh et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: C. trachomatis Cdu1 is a 401 amino acid protein with a single-pass transmembrane domain located towards the N-terminus and a predicted flexible area up to residue 167.
source: C. trachomatis Cdu1 is a 401 amino acid protein with a single-pass transmembrane domain located towards the N-terminus and a predicted flexible area up to residue 167.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis and structural prediction.

claim: In situ proteolysis and LCMS analysis identified a stable Cdu1 construct that displayed full proteolytic activity.
source: In situ proteolysis and LCMS analysis identified a stable Cdu1 construct that displayed full proteolytic activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) to pursue its structural characterization.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Cdu1 (155-401) fragment crystallized in space group P21 with two molecules in the asymmetric unit and at a resolution of 1.7 Å.
source: The Cdu1 (155-401) fragment crystallized in space group P21 (Supplementary file 1) with two molecules in the asymmetric unit and at a resolution of 1.7 Å.
evidence: This is a finding from the crystallographic analysis.

claim: Each monomer is composed of a central four-stranded β-sheet, which is surrounded by eight α-helixes resembling the architecture of the C48 proteases.
source: Each monomer is composed of a central four-stranded β-sheet, which is surrounded by eight α-helixes (Figure 2A) resembling the architecture of the C48 proteases.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The catalytic cysteine, Cys345, is located at the N-terminus of α-helix F.
source: The catalytic cysteine, Cys345, is located at the N-terminus of α-helix F, which is 'sandwiched' in between a set of three anti-parallel β-strands (1,2,3) and two extra α-helices, A and G, which are perpendicular to each other.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: β-strands 2 and 3 also contain the two other residues of the catalytic triad, His275 and Asp292.
source: β-strands 2 and 3 also contain the two other residues of the catalytic triad, His275 and Asp292.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The structure of Cdu1 was also solved by Pruneda et al. at a resolution of 2.1 Å.
source: Very recently, the structure of Cdu1 was also solved by Pruneda et al. at a resolution of 2.1 Å (Pruneda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The Pruneda et al. Cdu1 fragment consists of residues 130 to 401 and can be superimposed with our Cdu1 structure with an rms deviation of 0.563 Å including residues 161 to 401.
source: Their fragment consists of residues 130 to 401 and can be superimposed with our Cdu1 structure with an rms deviation of 0.563 Å including residues 161 to 401 using the program LSQ superpose in COOT (Kabsch, 1976).
evidence: This is a finding from structural comparison analysis.

claim: Due to the difference in length of the construct the structure of Pruneda et al. contains an additional α-helix at the N-terminus which is not present in our Cdu1 structure.
source: Due to the difference in length of the construct the structure of Pruneda et al. contains an additional α-helix at the N-terminus which is not present in our Cdu1 structure (Pruneda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from structural comparison analysis.

claim: Cdu1 (155-401) shares a high degree of structural similarity with Ulp1 despite the fact that they only share 17% sequence identity within a stretch of 221 amino acids.
source: A search for other related structures utilizing the program DALI (Holm and Sander, 1993) indicated that Cdu1 (155-401) shares a high degree of structural similarity with Ulp1 (Mossessova and Lima, 2000) despite the fact that they only share 17% sequence identity within a stretch of 221 amino acids.
evidence: This is a finding from structural comparison analysis.

claim: A small loop between β-strands 1 and 2 in Ulp1 contrasts with the much bigger α-helix D in Cdu1 in between the equivalent β-strands of both structures.
source: Remarkably, however, a small loop between β-strands 1 and 2 (shown in yellow) in Ulp1 contrasts with the much bigger α-helix D in Cdu1 (Figure 2A) in between the equivalent β-strands of both structures.
evidence: This is a finding from structural comparison analysis, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The residues within the active site are highly conserved.
source: In contrast to this difference, the residues within the active site are highly conserved (Figure 2D and E), further supporting the notion that Cdu1 forms a complex with ubiquitin in a similar way as observed between SENP8 and Nedd8 or Ulp1 and SMT3, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from structural comparison analysis, supported by Figure 2D and E.

claim: Cdu1 forms a complex with ubiquitin in a similar way as observed between SENP8 and Nedd8 or Ulp1 and SMT3.
source: In contrast to this difference, the residues within the active site are highly conserved (Figure 2D and E), further supporting the notion that Cdu1 forms a complex with ubiquitin in a similar way as observed between SENP8 and Nedd8 or Ulp1 and SMT3, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity and conservation of active site residues.

claim: The additional α-helix D in Cdu1, a feature not observed in the other structures, may play a regulatory role in substrate binding or recognition.
source: The additional α-helix D in Cdu1, a feature not observed in the other structures, however, may play a regulatory role in substrate binding or recognition.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observation of the unique α-helix D.

claim: Deletion of the α-helix D region (residues 250 to 272) prevented Cdu1 from binding ubiquitin/Nedd8 suicide probes.
source: This hypothesis is further strengthened by the analysis of Pruneda et al. where deletion of this region (residues 250 to 272) prevented Cdu1 from binding ubiquitin/Nedd8 suicide probes (Pruneda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: An insertion of identical length as observed in Cdu1 seems to be present in the Cdu1 proteins encoded by the genomes of C. suis, C. muridarum, C. psittaci, C. gallinaceai and Cdu2 from C. trachomatis suggesting that it is a conserved feature across the chlamydial deubiquitinases.
source: Importantly, an insertion of identical length as observed in Cdu1 seems to be present in the Cdu1 proteins encoded by the genomes of C. suis, C. muridarum, C. psittaci, C. gallinaceai and Cdu2 from C. trachomatis suggesting that it is a conserved feature across the chlamydial deubiquitinases (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A rabbit polyclonal antiserum directed against recombinant Cdu1 detected Cdu1 inside the inclusion 24 hpi co-localizing with bacterial particles.
source: A rabbit polyclonal antiserum directed against recombinant Cdu1 detected Cdu1 inside the inclusion 24 hpi co-localizing with bacterial particles.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: Major amounts of Cdu1 were also detected at the surface of the inclusion co-localizing with the inclusion membrane protein IncA.
source: Major amounts of Cdu1 were also detected at the surface of the inclusion co-localizing with the inclusion membrane protein IncA, where it might be anchored by its N-terminal transmembrane domain (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy, supported by Figure 3A and B.

claim: Cdu1 might be anchored at the surface of the inclusion by its N-terminal transmembrane domain.
source: Major amounts of Cdu1 were also detected at the surface of the inclusion co-localizing with the inclusion membrane protein IncA, where it might be anchored by its N-terminal transmembrane domain (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the presence of a transmembrane domain and the localization of Cdu1 at the inclusion surface.

claim: Cdu1 could not be detected in the host cell cytoplasm as it had been described before.
source: However, Cdu1 could not be detected in the host cell cytoplasm as it had been described before (Le Negrate et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy that contrasts with prior research.

claim: The expected arrangement of the cdu1 gene including the FLAG-tag at the C-terminus after recombination in the transformed new Chlamydia strain (Ctr Cdu1-FLAG) was verified by PCR and sequencing, as well as by Southern hybridization.
source: The expected arrangement of the cdu1 gene (Figure 3C) including the FLAG-tag at the C-terminus after recombination in the transformed new Chlamydia strain (Ctr Cdu1-FLAG) was verified by PCR and sequencing, as well as by Southern hybridization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from molecular biology experiments, supported by Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Ctr Cdu1-FLAG expressed only the FLAG-tagged version of Cdu1.
source: Ctr Cdu1-FLAG expressed only the FLAG-tagged version of Cdu1 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which was secreted to the surface of the inclusion (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot and immunofluorescence analysis, supported by Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, and Figure 3E.

claim: The FLAG-tagged Cdu1 was secreted to the surface of the inclusion.
source: Ctr Cdu1-FLAG expressed only the FLAG-tagged version of Cdu1 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which was secreted to the surface of the inclusion (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis, supported by Figure 3E.

claim: The accessibility of the C-terminal catalytic domain of Cdu1 to the host cell cytosol was demonstrated by antibody transfection experiments.
source: The accessibility of the C-terminal catalytic domain of Cdu1 to the host cell cytosol was demonstrated by antibody transfection experiments (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from antibody transfection experiments, supported by Figure 3F.

claim: Recombinant expression of Cdu1 in Chlamydia did not change its infectivity, as assessed by the efficiency and the duration of the developmental cycle.
source: Recombinant expression of Cdu1 in Chlamydia did not change its infectivity, as assessed by the efficiency and the duration of the developmental cycle, nor was the inhibition of host cell apoptosis affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is a finding from infectivity assays, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: The inhibition of host cell apoptosis was not affected by recombinant expression of Cdu1 in Chlamydia.
source: Recombinant expression of Cdu1 in Chlamydia did not change its infectivity, as assessed by the efficiency and the duration of the developmental cycle, nor was the inhibition of host cell apoptosis affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is a finding from apoptosis assays, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: The kinetics of Cdu1-FLAG expression and localization during the developmental cycle was not altered confirming the expression of the recombinant protein under the native promoter.
source: In addition, the kinetics of Cdu1-FLAG expression and localization during the developmental cycle was not altered confirming the expression of the recombinant protein under the native promoter (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from time course experiments, supported by Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Transcriptomics analysis of C. trachomatis-infected cells revealed that the insertion of the selection cassette at the cdu1 locus should not affect the downstream gene cdu2 since it is controlled by its own promoter.
source: Moreover, transcriptomics analysis of C. trachomatis-infected cells revealed that the insertion of the selection cassette at the cdu1 locus should not affect the downstream gene cdu2 since it is controlled by its own promoter (Albrecht et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mcl-1 is known to be located in the cytoplasm and to a certain degree in a complex with BAK at intracellular membranes.
source: Mcl-1 is known to be located in the cytoplasm and to a certain degree in a complex with BAK at intracellular membranes (Thomas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: This localization was confirmed by immunofluorescence staining of uninfected cells.
source: This localization was confirmed by immunofluorescence staining of uninfected cells.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: In C. trachomatis-infected cells high amounts of Mcl-1 were detected in close proximity to the inclusion.
source: Interestingly, in C. trachomatis-infected cells high amounts of Mcl-1 were detected in close proximity to the inclusion (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C) where Cdu1 is located (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy, supported by Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: This Mcl-1 Cdu1 co-localization was also detected in cells infected with Ctr Cdu1-FLAG.
source: This Mcl-1 Cdu1 co-localization was also detected in cells infected with Ctr Cdu1-FLAG (Figure 4C) or WT-infected cells expressing a GFP-Mcl-1 fusion protein (Figure 4D) ruling out unspecific binding of the antibody.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Mcl-1 Cdu1 co-localization was detected in WT-infected cells expressing a GFP-Mcl-1 fusion protein ruling out unspecific binding of the antibody.
source: This Mcl-1 Cdu1 co-localization was also detected in cells infected with Ctr Cdu1-FLAG (Figure 4C) or WT-infected cells expressing a GFP-Mcl-1 fusion protein (Figure 4D) ruling out unspecific binding of the antibody.
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy, supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Endogenous Mcl-1 precipitated together with Cdu1-FLAG from HeLa cells infected with Ctr Cdu1-FLAG.
source: The interaction of both proteins was then analyzed by co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous Mcl-1 together with Cdu1-FLAG from HeLa cells infected with Ctr Cdu1-FLAG (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Mcl-1 but not p53 precipitated together with Cdu1 confirming Cdu1 substrate specificity for Mcl-1.
source: Mcl-1 but not p53, another high turnover protein constantly targeted for ubiquitination, precipitated together with Cdu1 confirming Cdu1 substrate specificity for Mcl-1.
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments that demonstrates specificity.

claim: Endogenous Mcl-1 only co-precipitated together with Cdu1-FLAG but not with the other proteins from cells infected with the respective Chlamydia strain.
source: To rule out any non-specific binding of Mcl-1 to the FLAG-tag, HeLa cells were infected with C. trachomatis strains Ctr pTet/Cdu1-FLAG, Ctr pIncA-FLAG and Ctr pTet/Cdu2-FLAG overexpressing the indicated FLAG-tagged proteins. Endogenous Mcl-1 only co-precipitated together with Cdu1-FLAG but not with the other proteins from cells infected with the respective Chlamydia strain (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments, supported by Figure 4F.

claim: Overexpressed Cdu1-FLAG and endogenous Mcl-1 co-immunoprecipitated in uninfected HEK-293T cells.
source: Further proof was provided by co-immunoprecipitation of overexpressed Cdu1-FLAG and endogenous Mcl-1 in uninfected HEK-293T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GST-Mcl-1 bound exclusively to His-Cdu1, demonstrating a direct interaction of these two proteins.
source: GST-tagged Mcl-1 was bound to glutathione-sepharose beads and incubated with equal amounts of His-tagged Cdu1 or control proteins (His-Cdu2 and His-GroEL). GST-Mcl-1 bound exclusively to His-Cdu1, demonstrating a direct interaction of these two proteins (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro binding assays, supported by Figure 4G.

claim: Overexpression of Cdu1-FLAG led to a specific stabilization of Mcl-1.
source: Overexpression of Cdu1-FLAG led to a specific stabilization of Mcl-1 since Bcl-2, another anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family member, and several inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs) were not affected by Cdu1-FLAG overexpression (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from overexpression experiments, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Bcl-2 and several inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs) were not affected by Cdu1-FLAG overexpression.
source: Overexpression of Cdu1-FLAG led to a specific stabilization of Mcl-1 since Bcl-2, another anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family member, and several inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs) were not affected by Cdu1-FLAG overexpression (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from overexpression experiments, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Overexpression of the mutant Cdu1(C345A) could not stabilize Mcl-1 to the same extent as the wild-type enzyme.
source: Overexpression of the mutant Cdu1(C345A) could not stabilize Mcl-1 to the same extent as the wild-type enzyme (Figure 5A and B), suggesting that chlamydial Cdu1 alone is able to stabilize Mcl-1, very likely by deubiquitination.
evidence: This is a finding from overexpression experiments, supported by Figure 5A and B.

claim: Chlamydial Cdu1 alone is able to stabilize Mcl-1, very likely by deubiquitination.
source: Overexpression of the mutant Cdu1(C345A) could not stabilize Mcl-1 to the same extent as the wild-type enzyme (Figure 5A and B), suggesting that chlamydial Cdu1 alone is able to stabilize Mcl-1, very likely by deubiquitination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the catalytically inactive mutant cannot stabilize Mcl-1.

claim: The degree of poly-ubiquitination was higher if Mcl-1 was precipitated from cells co-transfected with the empty vector or inactive Cdu1(C345A)-FLAG compared to cells co-expressing Cdu1-FLAG.
source: The degree of poly-ubiquitination was higher if Mcl-1 was precipitated from cells co-transfected with the empty vector or inactive Cdu1(C345A)-FLAG compared to cells co-expressing Cdu1-FLAG (Figure 5C, left panel).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoprecipitation experiments, supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Cdu1, but not the control enzyme UCH-L3 strongly deubiquitinated Mcl-1.
source: Purified recombinant Mcl-1 was poly-ubiquitinated in vitro and was subsequently used as substrate for purified recombinant Cdu1, its mutant Cdu1(C345A) or the unrelated deubiquitinase UCH-L3. Cdu1, but not the control enzyme UCH-L3 strongly deubiquitinated Mcl-1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro deubiquitination assays, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: Deubiquitination of Mcl-1 was dependent on its enzymatic activity, since neither the Cdu1(C345A) mutant nor the wild-type enzyme blocked with the universal cysteine protease inhibitor N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) deubiquitinated Mcl-1.
source: Deubiquitination of Mcl-1 was dependent on its enzymatic activity, since neither the Cdu1(C345A) mutant nor the wild-type enzyme blocked with the universal cysteine protease inhibitor N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) deubiquitinated Mcl-1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro deubiquitination assays, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: Cdu1 specifically deubiquitinated Mcl-1 but not the control protein p53.
source: Furthermore, poly-ubiquitinated proteins were isolated by TUBE pull down and incubated with Cdu1 or the control DUB USP28. Cdu1 specifically deubiquitinated Mcl-1 but not the control protein p53 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro deubiquitination assays, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mcl-1 is primarily K48-ubiquitinated to target it to proteasomal degradation.
source: It has already been demonstrated in vitro that Cdu1 is a deubiquitinase and deneddylase (Misaghi et al., 2006). Mcl-1 is primarily K48-ubiquitinated to target it to proteasomal degradation (Mojsa et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cdu1 cleaves K48- and K63-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: We were able to show that Cdu1 cleaves K48- and K63-linked ubiquitin chains as it was recently described (Pruneda et al., 2016) (Figure 5E) supporting Mcl-1 being a substrate of Cdu1.
evidence: This is a finding from ubiquitin chain cleavage assays, supported by Figure 5E.

claim: One of the resulting mutant strains (Ctr cdu1::Tn bla), termed Ctr Tn-cdu1, had a transposon inserted in the active site of Cdu1, resulting in a truncated version with 297 amino acids and an apparent molecular weight of 33 kDa.
source: In another approach, transposon mutagenesis using a Himar1 transposon system was established in C. trachomatis. One of the resulting mutant strains (Ctr cdu1::Tn bla), termed Ctr Tn-cdu1, had a transposon inserted in the active site of Cdu1, resulting in a truncated version with 297 amino acids and an apparent molecular weight of 33 kDa (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from transposon mutagenesis, supported by Figure 6A and B.

claim: Comparison of the parental clone to the reference LGV 434/Bu genome revealed two mutations.
source: Comparison of the parental clone to the reference LGV 434/Bu genome revealed two mutations.
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

claim: One mutation (base 946,499) was in the coding region for CTL0818 (helicase) that resulted in an amino acid substitution (N1115H).
source: One mutation (base 946,499) was in the coding region for CTL0818 (helicase) that resulted in an amino acid substitution (N1115H).
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

claim: The other mutation was in CTL0817 (brnQ) and also resulted in a substitution (R275H).
source: The other was in CTL0817 (brnQ) and also resulted in a substitution (R275H).
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

source: Comparison of the Tn-cdu1 genome to the parental clone verified that the transposon is located as indicated in Figure 6A and introduces a Y298* non-sense mutation in cdu1.
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: Both sites in CTL0818 and CTL0817 that have mixed sequence in the parental strain, uniformly matched the reference strain.
source: Both sites in CTL0818 and CTL0817 that have mixed sequence in the parental strain, uniformly matched the reference strain; however, two new mutations were incurred in the Tn-cdu1 strain.
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

claim: Two new mutations were incurred in the Tn-cdu1 strain.
source: Both sites in CTL0818 and CTL0817 that have mixed sequence in the parental strain, uniformly matched the reference strain; however, two new mutations were incurred in the Tn-cdu1 strain.
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

claim: One mutation (base 929,586) occurred in the intergenic region between two diverging genes (CTL0805; hisS and CTL0806; uhpC).
source: One mutation (base 929,586) occurred in the intergenic region between two diverging genes (CTL0805; hisS and CTL0806; uhpC) and a missense mutation (base 11,738) was found in the gene encoding for RecC (CTL0008) and results in an amino acid substitution (S638Y).
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

claim: A missense mutation (base 11,738) was found in the gene encoding for RecC (CTL0008) and results in an amino acid substitution (S638Y).
source: One mutation (base 929,586) occurred in the intergenic region between two diverging genes (CTL0805; hisS and CTL0806; uhpC) and a missense mutation (base 11,738) was found in the gene encoding for RecC (CTL0008) and results in an amino acid substitution (S638Y).
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

claim: The genomes of the parent and Tn-cdu1 strain are almost identical with the exception of the transposon insertions.
source: Taken together, this analysis reveals that the genomes of the parent and Tn-cdu1 strain are almost identical with the exception of the transposon insertions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: The only modification to a coding region was in RecC (S638Y).
source: While there are two distinct mutations in the Tn-cdu1 clone relative to the parent clone, the only modification to a coding region was in RecC (S638Y).
evidence: This is a finding from whole genome sequencing.

claim: The phenotypes observed of the Tn-cdu1 insertional mutant clone are almost definitively due to the functional disruption of the Cdu1 deubiquitinase.
source: These data support that the phenotypes observed of the Tn-cdu1 insertional mutant clone are almost definitively due to the functional disruption of the Cdu1 deubiquitinase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic analysis showing minimal differences between parent and mutant strains.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of HeLa cells infected with the Ctr Tn-cdu1 mutant strain revealed reduced protein levels as well as impaired secretion of the truncated Cdu1 protein to the surface of the inclusion.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of HeLa cells infected with the Ctr Tn-cdu1 mutant strain revealed reduced protein levels as well as impaired secretion of the truncated Cdu1 protein to the surface of the inclusion (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy, supported by Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mcl-1 levels were reduced in cells infected with Ctr Tn-cdu1 compared to cells infected with wild-type bacteria.
source: Interestingly, Mcl-1 levels were reduced in cells infected with Ctr Tn-cdu1 compared to cells infected with wild-type bacteria (Figure 6B,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoblot analysis, supported by Figure 6B, D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Mcl-1 level did not decrease to the level detected in uninfected control cells highlighting that Chlamydia established multiple mechanisms to induce Mcl-1 accumulation in the cell.
source: However, the Mcl-1 level did not decrease to the level detected in uninfected control cells highlighting that Chlamydia established multiple mechanisms to induce Mcl-1 accumulation in the cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Mcl-1 levels remain elevated even in the Cdu1 mutant.

claim: Mcl-1 was less accumulated around the inclusion of the Ctr Tn-cdu1 mutant strain compared to wild-type Chlamydia-infected cells.
source: Moreover, Mcl-1 was less accumulated around the inclusion of the Ctr Tn-cdu1 mutant strain compared to wild-type Chlamydia-infected cells (Figure 6E–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Mcl-1 is still recruited to the inclusion of Tn-cdu1 Chlamydia, however, the amount of inclusion-associated Mcl-1 is decreased in Ctr Tn-cdu1-infected cells compared to the WT.

evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy, supported by Figure 6G.

claim: Chlamydial overexpression of Cdu1 resulted in a slight increase in Mcl-1 accumulation around the inclusion.
source: Furthermore, chlamydial overexpression of Cdu1 resulted in a slight increase in Mcl-1 accumulation around the inclusion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C.

claim: Mcl-1 isolated from cells infected with the mutant bacteria is more ubiquitinated, in particular K48-linked ubiquitinated, compared to the Ctr wild-type-infected sample.
source: The analysis of the ubiquitination pattern of Mcl-1 isolated from cells infected with wild-type or Tn-cdu1 mutant Chlamydia clearly showed that Mcl-1 isolated from cells infected with the mutant bacteria is more ubiquitinated, in particular K48-linked ubiquitinated, compared to the Ctr wild-type-infected sample (Figure 7A, left panel and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoprecipitation and immunoblot analysis, supported by Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mcl-1 still shows reduced ubiquitination in comparison to the uninfected control, which could be a result of the sequestration of Mcl-1 to the inclusion.
source: However, Mcl-1 still shows reduced ubiquitination in comparison to the uninfected control, which could be a result of the sequestration of Mcl-1 to the inclusion (see Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of reduced ubiquitination even in the mutant.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining for ubiquitin or K48-linked ubiquitin and Mcl-1 in Ctr Tn-cdu1-infected cells shows that ubiquitin is accumulating around the inclusion in part co-localizing with Mcl-1.
source: Indeed, immunofluorescence staining for ubiquitin or K48-linked ubiquitin and Mcl-1 in Ctr Tn-cdu1-infected cells shows that ubiquitin is accumulating around the inclusion in part co-localizing with Mcl-1 (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence microscopy, supported by Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Using structured illumination microscopy (SIM), we show that the inclusion-associated Mcl-1 is strongly ubiquitinated in Ctr Tn-cdu1-infected cells in comparison to cells infected with wild-type Chlamydia.
source: Using structured illumination microscopy (SIM), we show that the inclusion-associated Mcl-1 is strongly ubiquitinated in Ctr Tn-cdu1-infected cells in comparison to cells infected with wild-type Chlamydia.
evidence: This is a finding from super-resolution microscopy.

claim: The increase in the ubiquitination of Mcl-1 is exhibited by the rise in the degree of co-localization as shown by Pearson's co-localization analysis.
source: The increase in the ubiquitination of Mcl-1 is exhibited by the rise in the degree of co-localization as shown by Pearson's co-localization analysis (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from co-localization analysis, supported by Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The Ctr Tn-cdu1 mutant strain did not show any sensitization towards apoptosis induction compared to the wild-type Chlamydia.
source: We challenged the transposon mutant Chlamydia with TNFα/CHX in an apoptosis assay, however, the Cdu1 mutant did not show any sensitization towards apoptosis induction compared to the wild-type Chlamydia (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from apoptosis assays, supported by Figure 7D.

claim: In cells infected with Ctr Tn-cdu1 the MEK/ERK survival signaling pathway was still activated and Mcl-1 levels were increased which may compensate for the lack of Mcl-1 stabilization by Cdu1.
source: In cells infected with Ctr Tn-cdu1 the MEK/ERK survival signaling pathway was still activated and Mcl-1 levels were increased which may compensate for the lack of Mcl-1 stabilization by Cdu1 (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the mutant does not sensitize to apoptosis despite reduced Mcl-1 stabilization.

claim: The Ctr Tn-cdu1 mutant strain showed a sensitization toward immune stimulation with interferon (IFN) γ, which became evident by a significant reduction of replication in primary cells of human fimbriae obtained from biopsies (referred as Fimb cells) reflecting the natural infection site for C. trachomatis after IFNγ treatment.
source: On the contrary, the Ctr Tn-cdu1 mutant strain showed a sensitization toward immune stimulation with interferon (IFN) γ, which became evident by a significant reduction of replication in primary cells of human fimbriae obtained from biopsies (referred as Fimb cells) reflecting the natural infection site for C. trachomatis after IFNγ treatment (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding from infectivity assays, supported by Figure 7E.

claim: Statistical analysis of the bacterial burdens of WT to Tn-IGR infected mice revealed no significant difference with mean genome ratios of 5.4 × 10−3 and 4.4 × 10−3, respectively.
source: Statistical analysis of the bacterial burdens of WT to Tn-IGR infected mice revealed no significant difference with mean genome ratios of 5.4 × 10−3 and 4.4 × 10−3, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from mouse infection experiments.

source: In contrast, statistical analysis revealed a highly significant difference (p<0.01) in bacterial burdens with over a log fold decrease in mean bacterial burden (2.0 × 10−4) of Tn-cdu1.
evidence: This is a finding from mouse infection experiments.

claim: These observations support the hypothesis that Cdu1 is important during mammalian infection.
source: These observations support the hypothesis that Cdu1 is important during mammalian infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mouse infection data.

claim: The chlamydial inclusion is the interface to the eukaryotic host and serves as a signaling platform that orchestrates the accommodation of this obligate intracellular bacterium inside the host cell.
source: The chlamydial inclusion is the interface to the eukaryotic host and serves as a signaling platform that orchestrates the accommodation of this obligate intracellular bacterium inside the host cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chlamydial inclusion.

claim: Numerous secreted chlamydial proteins decorate the inclusion surface and function as scaffolds that recruit host trafficking and signaling molecules to the inclusion.
source: Numerous secreted chlamydial proteins decorate the inclusion surface and function as scaffolds that recruit host trafficking and signaling molecules to the inclusion (Elwell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: We demonstrate here the localization of the chlamydial deubiquitinating enzyme Cdu1 to the inclusion surface and its essential role for chlamydial development in IFNγ-challenged cultured cells and in a mouse infection model.
source: We demonstrate here the localization of the chlamydial deubiquitinating enzyme Cdu1 to the inclusion surface and its essential role for chlamydial development in IFNγ-challenged cultured cells and in a mouse infection model.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: This is the first report on a functionally and structurally eukaryotic-like enzyme encoded and secreted by Chlamydia that is required for the adaptation and survival of these bacteria.
source: This is the first report on a functionally and structurally eukaryotic-like enzyme encoded and secreted by Chlamydia that is required for the adaptation and survival of these bacteria.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: We further show that Cdu1 specifically deubiquitinates the major apoptosis regulator Mcl-1 at the surface of the inclusion.
source: We further show that Cdu1 specifically deubiquitinates the major apoptosis regulator Mcl-1 at the surface of the inclusion.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claim: Due to the high turn-over rate of Mcl-1, actively growing Chlamydia have to interfere with a very well-balanced cellular system consisting of several Mcl-1-specific ubiquitin ligases and the deubiquitinating enzyme USP9X that constantly tune the levels of Mcl-1.
source: Due to the high turn-over rate of Mcl-1, actively growing Chlamydia have to interfere with a very well-balanced cellular system consisting of several Mcl-1-specific ubiquitin ligases and the deubiquitinating enzyme USP9X (Schwickart et al., 2010; Zhong et al., 2005; Thomas et al., 2010) that constantly tune the levels of Mcl-1.

claim: Early in infection, expression of Mcl-1 is increased by the activation of the RAF/MEK/ERK and the MAPK/AKT signaling pathway.
source: Early in infection, expression of Mcl-1 is increased by the activation of the RAF/MEK/ERK and the MAPK/AKT signaling pathway (Rajalingam et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Maintenance of increased Mcl-1 levels in the mid and late phases of infection, however, required in addition stabilization of the protein.
source: Maintenance of increased Mcl-1 levels in the mid and late phases of infection, however, required in addition stabilization of the protein.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: We show here that Mcl-1 stabilization is a result of reduced ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation induced by the chlamydial Cdu1 that is independent of the known major host UPS factors regulating Mcl-1 stability.
source: We show here that Mcl-1 stabilization is a result of reduced ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation induced by the chlamydial Cdu1 that is independent of the known major host UPS factors regulating Mcl-1 stability.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claim: Mcl-1 may be just one of several Cdu1 targets that are deubiquitinated in infected cells.
source: Mcl-1 may be just one of several Cdu1 targets that are deubiquitinated in infected cells.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential additional Cdu1 substrates.

source: Furthermore, with the exception of Cdu2, Cdu1 is the only known bacterial DUB that possesses both deubiquitinating and deneddylating activities (Misaghi et al., 2006) indicating that also Cdus' deneddylating activity may be relevant for the intracellular adaptation of the pathogen.

source: Since previous work on the cellular Mcl-1 deubiquitinase USP9X demonstrated that deubiquitinase and target do not have to reside in the same cellular compartment (Schwickart et al., 2010) it can be speculated, that inclusion-associated Cdu1 constantly increases the pool of cytosolic Mcl-1 and thereby also the amount of effective anti-apoptotic Mcl-1 at the mitochondria.

source: Our co-localization analysis using SIM clearly demonstrated reduced ubiquitinated Mcl-1 at the inclusion surface of wild-type Chlamydia compared to inclusions of the Tn-cdu1 mutant strain (Figure 7C).

claim: Although the integration of a FLAG-tagged version of Cdu1 into the C. trachomatis genome replacing the wild-type gene was effective, generating a knock-out by deleting or interrupting the cdu1 gene close to the N-terminus was not successful.
source: Although the integration of a FLAG-tagged version of Cdu1 into the C. trachomatis genome replacing the wild-type gene was effective, generating a knock-out by deleting or interrupting the cdu1 gene close to the N-terminus was not successful.

source: The isolation of Tn-cdu1 demonstrated that at least the catalytic activity of Cdu1 is not essential for chlamydial growth in cultured cells.

source: While it is unknown what specific aspect of infection is affected by this genetic disruption, a polar effect of the transposon insertion on genes downstream of the Cdu1 coding gene is unlikely, since cdu2 (Cdu2) is directly downstream of cdu1 and has been shown to have its own transcriptional start site (Albrecht et al., 2010).

claim: Mcl-1 still localizes to the inclusion in the cdu1 allelic replacement strain (Ctr Cdu1-FLAG).
